extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in U.S. free-speech law, media scholars, journalists and policy watchers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedia-style overview of censorship and free-speech-related legal standards, corporate practices, and historical examples in the United States. Covers judicial tests, statutory rules, administrative practice, and documented forms of corporate/self-censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, place, and manner (TPM) restriction lawfulness criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: TPM restrictions, as these are known, are only lawful when: they treat all speech equally; they are justified by a substantial, bona-fide public interest, such as crowd control; they do not substantively impede or dilute the speech at hand; there is no bad faith; there is no overt or ulterior motive by the authorities imposing a TPM restriction to suppress speech in general, or speech that they disagree with, in particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All TPM restrictions are subject to judicial review. Unreasonable and unconstitutional TPM restrictions have been vacated or enjoined by courts. TPM restrictions related to core political speech are subject to the highest possible level of Constitutional scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free speech zones / First Amendment zones requirements and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Free speech zones are areas set aside in public places for political activism based on the government's authority to regulate time, place, and manner but not content. Their stated purpose is to protect safety of attendees or protesters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are lawful only when they meet TPM criteria (content neutrality, substantial public interest, do not dilute speech, no bad faith). Critics argue they are used to remove protesters from sight of media ('Orwellian'); courts and civil liberties groups (e.g., ACLU, FIRE) have litigated abuses. Use at universities and political gatherings has prompted lawsuits and objections when implemented to curtail visibility of protesters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on material support for foreign boycotts (TRA / EAR guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1977 U.S. law penalizes U.S. persons (including companies and their foreign affiliates) from supporting a boycott of Israel and lists conduct that may be penalized under the TRA and/or prohibited under the EAR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct listed includes: agreements to refuse or actual refusal to do business with or in Israel or with blacklisted companies; agreements to discriminate or actual discrimination based on race, religion, sex, national origin or nationality; agreements to furnish or actual furnishing of information about business relationships with or in Israel or with blacklisted companies; agreements to furnish or actual furnishing of information about the race, religion, sex, or national origin of another person; implementing letters of credit containing prohibited boycott terms or conditions. The TRA does not literally 'prohibit' conduct but denies tax benefits (i.e., penalizes) certain boycott-related agreements. The law forbids material participation in or material support of a boycott originated by a foreign nation or organization, not domestic boycotts, and does not prohibit merely political or moral support for a boycott. Material attempts to suppress speech by falsely claiming domestic boycotts are foreign in origin may be unlawful and can constitute federal crimes such as conspiracy against civil rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of unprotected or partially protected speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of speech can be totally or partially abridged under federal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include perjury, fraud, obscenity, and defamation. Although the First Amendment generally forbids laws abridging speech, these categories have been recognized as outside full First Amendment protection and subject to regulation or punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel standard for public figures (New York Times Co. v. Sullivan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the 1964 New York Times Co. v. Sullivan decision, public figures (entertainers, politicians, etc.) must prove actual malice — i.e., that the defendant acted with knowledge of falsity or with reckless disregard for the truth — rather than mere negligence to win a libel or slander suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While difficult to win a libel case, civil suits can still intimidate because defending them is expensive and time-consuming. Additionally, criminal libel laws remain on the books in some states (about 24 as of the article) and can be used occasionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: DMCA anti-circumvention standard and research exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, circumvention of a technological measure that effectively controls access to a work is illegal if done with the primary intent of violating the rights of copyright holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DMCA contains an exception for research, but the law has had a chilling effect on cryptography and security research (examples: arrest of Dmitry Sklyarov; reluctance of researchers like Niels Ferguson and some academics to publish findings). Free-speech lawsuits have arisen around publication of encryption keys (DeCSS, AACS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior restraint doctrine (Near v. Minnesota)
rubrics_metrics.description: Near v. Minnesota (1931) established the doctrine that prior restraint — censorship that prevents material from being published in the first place — is in most cases unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior restraint is distinguished from punishment after publication (which is an alternative). The doctrine has been central to protecting press freedom against government attempts to block publication; exceptions are narrow and courts apply strict scrutiny to prior restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedition and incitement tests (clear-and-present-danger; imminent lawless action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and constitutional tests determine when advocacy or speech can be criminalized: Schenck v. United States applied the 'clear and present danger' test; Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) established the 'imminent lawless action' test, which is the modern standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes like the Smith Act (Alien Registration Act, 18 U.S.C. § 2385) criminalize knowingly or willfully advocating overthrow of the government; the Smith Act was used extensively in mid-20th century prosecutions but many convictions were later overturned as unconstitutional under evolving First Amendment doctrine. Modern doctrine generally requires advocacy to be directed to and likely to produce imminent lawless action to be punishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial orders limiting publication (gag orders, record sealing) and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual judges can issue gag orders or order record sealing to prevent disclosure of information that might interfere with an ongoing case or to protect sensitive information; however, such powers are subject to strict review by higher courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nebraska Press Assn. v. Stuart established a high standard that must be met for courts to prevent media organizations from publishing information to preserve a defendant's right to a fair trial. Such orders are generally narrower in the U.S. than in some other common-law countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate censorship and self-censorship dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate censorship in news and entertainment often takes the form of self-censorship: journalists and editors avoid controversial reporting or 'soften' stories to avoid trouble with employers, advertisers, or powerful interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars note this is hard to document because it is covert — 'the dog that didn’t bark' — but surveys and studies report substantial incidence (studies cited report more than 40% of journalists and news executives admitting to deliberate self-censorship by avoiding stories or softening tones). Self-censorship accumulates through many small daily decisions rather than dramatic conspiracies; it can lead to 'homogenized, corporate-friendly media.'
